options.text: One species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced
options.explanation: The split into two directions is the defining signature.
That is ordinary redox between partners.

options.text: A species neither gains nor loses electrons
options.explanation: No transfer means no redox at all.
Displacement is a different reaction family.

questions.stem: In chlorine water, which products does chlorine divide into?

options.explanation: Oxygen is not the split partner here.
One leg down, one leg up from 0.
The second product must carry a different state.
That belongs to the hot-alkali case, not chlorine water.

questions.stem: Why must the starting oxidation state sit between the two product states?

options.explanation: Physical state is irrelevant.

options.text: So the equation balances by mass
options.explanation: Mass balance is automatic; the state geometry is the point.

options.text: One leg must go up and one leg down for simultaneous oxidation and reduction
options.explanation: The split requires an accessible state on both sides.
No such prohibition exists.

questions.stem: Which statement about the electron ledger in disproportionation is correct?

options.text: External ions supply the missing electrons
options.explanation: No external partner exists.

options.text: Electrons appear as free particles in the products
options.explanation: Electrons never appear in balanced equations.

options.text: The legs run in separate vessels
options.explanation: The legs run in one reaction mixture.

options.text: Electrons lost on the oxidation leg exactly equal those gained on the reduction leg
options.explanation: The ledger closes inside one species.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT required to identify a reaction as disproportionation?

options.text: A metal catalyst speeding the reaction
options.explanation: Catalysis plays no role in the definition.

options.text: A single species containing the element
options.explanation: The reactant must hold one relevant species.

options.text: One product at a higher oxidation number
options.explanation: The upward leg is required.

options.text: One product at a lower oxidation number
options.explanation: The downward leg is required.

questions.stem: State the definition of a disproportionation reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Disproportionation is the reaction type in which a single species is oxidised and reduced at the same instant, splitting one element across two products.

questions.stem: Give the two oxidation numbers chlorine lands on in chlorine water.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorine lands on -1 as chloride and +1 as chlorate(I), split from its starting 0.

questions.stem: Explain why disproportionation needs no external oxidising or reducing agent.
questions.modelAnswer: The species supplies both roles: some of its atoms lose electrons and some gain them, so the electron ledger closes internally within one reactant.

questions.stem: Chlorine water splits Cl at 0 into -1 and +1. If one chlorine atom oxidises by 1 unit, how many must reduce by 1 unit to close the ledger?
questions.modelAnswer: One atom losing 1 electron feeds exactly one atom gaining 1 electron, so the split is one-to-one in that case.

questions.stem: In hot concentrated NaOH, chlorine ends as which two ions?

options.explanation: Those are reactants, not products.
Chloride and chlorate(V) are the hot-alkali destinations.
That is the cold, dilute alkali case.
No hydrogen product appears in this reaction.

questions.stem: Which oxidation-number changes drive the balancing?

options.explanation: Oxygen stays -2 throughout.
Sodium is a spectator ion here.

options.text: Chlorine falls 0 to -1 and climbs 0 to +5
options.explanation: One down-leg and one up-leg define the split.
Disproportionation needs both legs.

questions.stem: Why does the 5Cl- to 1ClO3- ratio appear in the balanced equation?

options.explanation: Mass plays no role in the ratio's origin.

options.text: The chlorate ion holds five oxygens
options.explanation: It holds three, and oxygens do not set the ratio.
The alkali supplies charge balance, not the chlorine headcount.

options.text: One chlorine climbs 5 units, so five chlorines must each fall 1 unit to balance the ledger
options.explanation: The electron ledger fixes the headcount.

questions.stem: How many hydroxide ions appear on the reactant side, and why?

options.text: Six, matching the six negative charges among the products
options.explanation: Step 4 patches charge with hydroxide.
The waters belong to step 5, not the charge patch.
The chlorides carry only part of the product charge.
The ionic form exposes the hydroxide's role.

questions.stem: What final census verifies the balanced equation 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O?

options.explanation: Both atoms and charges must close.

options.text: 6 chlorine, 6 oxygen and 6 hydrogen atoms on each side
options.explanation: The full atom census closes on both sides.
Three Cl2 molecules hold six atoms.
Three waters plus one chlorate hold six.

questions.stem: List the five steps for balancing a disproportionation equation.
questions.modelAnswer: Write the unbalanced equation, deduce the oxidation-number changes, balance the number changes, balance the charges, then balance the atoms.

questions.stem: Write the balanced equation for chlorine in hot concentrated sodium hydroxide.
questions.modelAnswer: 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O closes the chlorine, oxygen and hydrogen censuses.

questions.stem: Explain why the hot-alkali product differs from the cold-dilute product.
questions.modelAnswer: Reaction conditions decide which split chlorine takes: hot concentrated alkali pushes the oxidation leg all the way to chlorate(V) at +5, while cold dilute alkali stops it at chlorate(I) at +1.

questions.stem: In the balanced hot-alkali equation, how many electrons move in total per 3 chlorine molecules reacting?
questions.modelAnswer: Five atoms fall 1 unit and one climbs 5, so 5 electrons shift per 6 chlorine atoms - matching a 5-unit up-leg and 5-unit down-leg total.
